questions.q: In Young's experiment, what is meant by the path difference between two rays that meet at a point on the screen?
options: The difference in brightness between the central maximum and the first dark band
The difference between the lengths of the two paths the waves travel from the source through one pinhole or the other
The angle between the straight-through direction and the line to the bright spot
The separation between the two pinholes in the card
questions.explanation: The textbook defines the path difference as the difference between the lengths of the two alternative routes light travels, through one pinhole or the other, to reach a point on the screen. When the crests from one pinhole meet the troughs from the other (exactly out of phase) the waves interfere destructively and a dark band appears.

questions.q: According to the textbook, the condition for constructive interference (a maximum) is that the path difference d sin θ equals what?
options: A whole number minus one half, multiplied by the wavelength: (m − ½)λ
A whole number multiple of the wavelength, mλ, giving d sin θ = mλ
The slit separation divided by the wavelength, d/λ
The distance x to the band divided by the screen distance L
questions.explanation: The textbook shows that the extra distance travelled by ray D2 equals the path difference d sin θ by trigonometry, and that constructive interference (a maximum, a bright band) occurs when this path difference is a whole number multiple of the wavelength. Hence d sin θ = mλ. Destructive interference (a minimum) instead occurs when d sin θ = (m − ½)λ.

questions.q: A sodium lamp produces almost-monochromatic light of wavelength 589 nm falling on two parallel vertical slits 0.100 mm apart, forming an interference pattern on a screen 1.50 m away. Determine the angle of the first-order maximum.
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's Sample Problem 1. Rearranging d sin θ = mλ gives sin θ = mλ/d, and the inverse sine gives 0.337°. Because this is a tiny angle, the small-angle approximation is safe, so the distance on the screen is x = L sin θ = 1.5 × 5.89 × 10⁻³ = 8.8 mm.

questions.q: White light strikes a diffraction grating of line separation d = 10 μm. Using d sin θ = mλ, find the first-order angle for red light of wavelength 700 nm.
questions.explanation: These are the textbook's white-light dispersion values. Red light (700 nm) gives 4.0°, while blue light (450 nm) gives only 2.6°, because the longer wavelength sits in the numerator and is diffracted to a larger angle. So each maximum is dispersed into a spectrum running from blue nearest the centre out to red — the opposite order to a prism.

questions.q: Why does a diffraction grating produce a sharper, better-separated pattern of maxima than a double slit?
options: It uses light of a shorter wavelength
The larger the number of slits (lines) on the grating, the sharper the image, producing a well-separated pattern of narrow peaks
The lines are spaced much further apart than double-slit slits
It only allows the central maximum through and blocks all other orders
questions.explanation: The textbook states that a grating consists of a large number of equidistant parallel lines, and that the larger the number of slits on a grating, the sharper the image obtained. The many ruled lines act as point sources whose interference produces a well-separated pattern of narrow, sharp peaks — which is why gratings are used in spectrometers.

questions.q: A diffraction grating is quoted as N lines per centimetre. According to the textbook investigation, how is the slit separation d in metres found from N?
options: \(d = \dfrac{1}{100\,N}\) — the reciprocal of the lines per metre
\(d = N\) (the line number is the separation)
questions.explanation: The textbook gives the relationship between the number of lines per centimetre on the grating N and the distance d between the lines as d = 1/(100N). The factor of 100 converts lines per centimetre to lines per metre before taking the reciprocal — forgetting it leaves your answer wrong by a factor of a hundred.

questions.q: From memory: summarise what the chapter review says happens to the maxima when white light, rather than monochromatic light, passes through a diffraction grating.
keyPoints: A diffraction grating is a piece of glass with many fine lines ruled upon it (thousands of lines per centimetre), producing a very sharp interference pattern.
If white light is used, each maximum is dispersed into a spectrum.
This happens because each wavelength of light has a different diffraction angle (from d sin θ = mλ).
questions.explanation: The review summary states that when white light is used, each maximum is dispersed into a spectrum since each wavelength of light has a different diffraction angle. If you recalled the dispersion of each maximum and tied it to a wavelength-dependent angle, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: A grating throws a first-order maximum out to 9° from the centre. To find the distance x from the central maximum to that spot on a screen distance L away, what should you do?
options: Use the small-angle approximation x = mλL/d, since it always holds
Use d sin θ = mλ to find the angle, then x = L tan θ for the screen distance, because at large angles sin θ ≠ tan θ
Use x = L sin θ, because the sine is always correct for the screen distance
Use x = L/tan θ, the reciprocal of the geometry
questions.explanation: The small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ x/L only holds for a few degrees. Gratings often produce wide angles where sine and tangent differ noticeably, so you must use d sin θ = mλ for the angle and then x = L tan θ for the screen distance. Sine inside the grating equation, tangent for the screen distance once the angle is large.

questions.q: From memory: state the safe sequence for finding the slit separation d when a grating is quoted in lines per centimetre, and the two classic errors it prevents.
keyPoints: Convert lines per centimetre to lines per metre first by multiplying by 100 (there are 100 cm in a metre).
Then take the reciprocal: d = 1 / (lines per metre). 'Convert, then reciprocate, in that order.'
This avoids the two classic errors: treating the line number itself as d (no reciprocal), and forgetting the ×100 conversion (off by a factor of 100).
questions.explanation: The episode's slogan is 'Centimetres? Times a hundred, then flip.' For example, 5000 lines/cm → 500 000 lines/m → d = 1/500 000 = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. If you recalled both the ×100 conversion and the reciprocal, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Analyse the factors involved in the production of an interference pattern from a double slit and a diffraction grating, using d sin θ = mλ. (6 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The condition for a bright fringe in both devices is d sin θ = mλ, where d is the slit or line separation, θ the angle to the fringe, m the integer order and λ the wavelength. Solving for sin θ = mλ/d: (1) the slit separation d is in the denominator, so decreasing d increases the angle to each fringe and spreads the pattern out — a grating with more lines per millimetre has a smaller d and a more spread-out pattern. (2) The wavelength λ is in the numerator, so a longer wavelength gives a larger angle; with white light, red is diffracted more than violet, so each order disperses into a spectrum with violet nearest the centre and red furthest out — the opposite order to a prism. (3) The order m is also in the numerator, so successive maxima appear at progressively larger angles. Comparing the devices: a double slit has only two coherent sources and produces broad, fuzzy maxima, whereas a diffraction grating has thousands of coherent sources that produce much sharper, narrower, brighter and better-separated maxima at the same fringe positions, which is why gratings are used in spectrometers to resolve closely spaced spectral lines.

criteria.descriptor: States d sin θ = mλ and analyses the effect of d (denominator → smaller d spreads the pattern).
Analyses wavelength (numerator → longer λ larger angle) and order m, including white-light dispersion and the prism contrast.
Compares double slit (two sources, broad fuzzy maxima) with grating (thousands of sources, sharper, better-resolved maxima) tied to resolution.

questions.explanation: A full-mark analyse answer ties every factor to its position in the equation (Distant Light Marches Outward) and uses the 'whereas' signpost to contrast the double slit with the grating (Many Sources, Sharp Lines).
